# Guardrails and Human Oversight {#sec-guardrails}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One measurement, entirely deterministic and with no
model in it: four Turkish PII detectors over a 480-message corpus whose planted
identifiers are known by construction, scored on precision and recall. It exists
to make one argument concrete — that a guardrail's failure mode is not "it
missed something" but "it missed something *and* you cannot tell". Software:
Python 3.14.5 standard library only, no third-party dependencies.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- say what a guardrail is for, and why it is not a security boundary;
- build a PII detector that validates, and know what validation costs you;
- redact reversibly, so a masked conversation can still do useful work;
- classify every action a system can take by whether it can be undone;
- design an approval gate that interrupts, reviews and resumes;
- write the runbook for an agent that is misbehaving at 3am;
- turn an incident into a regression test rather than a document nobody reads.

## Guardrails are risk reduction, not a security boundary {#sec-guardrails-boundary}

Start with the distinction that everything else depends on, because getting it
wrong is how teams end up with a false sense of safety.

A **guardrail** reduces the rate and severity of bad outcomes from a system that
is behaving normally: a user pastes a national ID into a chat, a model drifts
into advice it should not give, an agent tries to issue a refund larger than
anyone intended. The adversary here is entropy — users doing unusual things,
models being wrong, edge cases nobody enumerated.

A **security boundary** holds against someone actively trying to break it. That
is @sec-agent-security's subject, and the technique that defeats most guardrails
is embarrassingly simple: try again, slightly differently.

A terminology note before the table, because the word is used more broadly
elsewhere: in this book a **guardrail** is a filter that decides by inference —
a classifier, a judge, a heuristic — and a **boundary** is a rule the runtime
enforces regardless of what any model said. A deterministic check can be either,
depending on where it sits: the TCKN checksum later in this chapter is exact
arithmetic, and it is still a guardrail, because what it feeds is a redaction
decision rather than a permission. Elsewhere you will see "guardrail" cover both;
what matters is the distinction, not the label. Deterministic is also not the
same as error-free: an exact check can still have false positives and false
negatives against what you meant it to catch.

[The guardrails in this sense are probabilistic filters, so an attacker gets
unlimited retries against a component that is right most of the time.]{.hl}
"Most of the time" is a
fine property for reducing accidental harm and a useless one for stopping
deliberate harm. The practical consequence is architectural: a guardrail belongs
*in front of* a permission system, never *instead of* one. If the only thing
stopping an agent from issuing a €50,000 refund is a classifier that usually
notices, the refund limit is not enforced.

| | guardrail | boundary |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **stops** | accidents, drift, unusual inputs | deliberate attempts |
| **built from** | classifiers, regexes, prompts, judges | permissions, allowlists, capability limits |
| **fails** | probabilistically, and quietly | by design, loudly or not at all — in practice, only as well as it is implemented, so a boundary needs its own tests |
| **retries help the attacker** | yes — this is the whole problem | no |
| **evidence it works** | measured false-positive and false-negative rates | an argument about what is reachable |

: Two different jobs, routinely conflated {tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

The rest of this chapter is about building guardrails well, on the understanding
that building them well does not turn them into boundaries.

## What a PII detector actually has to do {#sec-guardrails-pii}

The most common guardrail is also the one most often shipped broken, because it
looks finished long before it is. Detecting personal data in Turkish support
traffic makes a good worked example: the identifiers have published check
digits, so correctness is verifiable rather than a matter of taste.

The corpus is 480 synthetic Turkish support messages built from eight templates
with randomised slots. Ground truth is known by construction: **360 national ID numbers (TCKN)** and **120 IBANs** are planted. Each planted
identifier independently receives a single-digit typo with probability 0.15, so
the *realised* rates are **55 of 360 (15.3%)** for TCKN and **15 of 120
(12.5%)** for IBAN. That distinction matters below, because every recall figure
in this section is measured against the realised rate rather than the nominal
one. Alongside them sit
**540 eleven-digit strings that are not national IDs**: mobile numbers written
without spaces, order references, cargo tracking codes, invoice numbers, meter
readings. That collision is the entire problem. A Turkish mobile number written
`05xxxxxxxxx` is exactly eleven digits, and so is a TCKN.

Four detectors, each a superset or filter of the pattern:

```text
TCKN, 480 messages, 360 planted, 540 eleven-digit decoys

  detector                      hits   correct   precision   recall
  pattern only                   900       360       40.0%   100.0%
  pattern + checksum             308       305       99.0%    84.7%
  pattern + context word         180       180      100.0%    50.0%
  pattern + (checksum OR word)   340       337       99.1%    93.6%
```

### The naive detector is wrong six times out of ten

An eleven-digit regex finds every planted TCKN — recall 100%, which is the
number people report — and **60% of what it returns is not a national ID**. If
that detector drives redaction, it masks order numbers and phone numbers, and
the support agent reading the masked ticket cannot do their job. If it drives an
alert, the alert is ignored within a week.

[Precision, not recall, is what determines whether a guardrail survives contact
with the people who have to use it.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
The 40% figure depends on how many decoys the corpus contains — 1.5 per planted
identifier here, a number I chose. The direction is robust and the magnitude is
not; measure it on your own traffic.
:::

### Validation buys precision, and takes something real

TCKN has a published two-digit checksum. Applying it lifts precision from 40% to
**99.0%**, which is the result everybody expects, and costs **15.3 points of
recall**, which is the result nobody plans for.

::: {.column-margin}
**The rule.** An eleven-digit string $d_1 \ldots d_{11}$ is a valid TCKN when
$d_1 \neq 0$ and

$$d_{10} = \big(7(d_1{+}d_3{+}d_5{+}d_7{+}d_9) - (d_2{+}d_4{+}d_6{+}d_8)\big)
\bmod 10$$

$$d_{11} = \Big(\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{10} d_i\Big) \bmod 10$$

Both check digits are determined by the first nine, which is why the check costs
exactly two digits of the eleven-digit space. IBAN's is ISO 7064 mod-97: move
the first four characters to the end, map letters to numbers (A = 10 … Z = 35),
and require the resulting integer to be congruent to 1 modulo 97.
:::

Look at what it drops. The detector found 305 of the 360 planted identifiers,
and 305 is exactly the number of planted identifiers that are not mistyped. The
recall loss is not approximately the typo rate; it *is* the typo rate — and
that is a theorem rather than a measurement. The eleventh digit is the sum of
the first ten modulo ten, so changing any single digit shifts that sum and the
check *always* fails. Exhaustively: across every single-digit substitution on
20,000 valid numbers, 0 of 1.96 million passed.

Which sharpens the caveat rather than the finding. The typo model here is a
single random digit, and that is precisely the error class a checksum is
designed to catch every time. Give it a more realistic mistake — two adjacent
digits transposed — and the equality breaks: the eleventh digit does not change
at all under a swap, the tenth shifts by $8(b-a)$, and that is zero whenever
$b-a \equiv 0 \pmod 5$. Measured over 178,000 transpositions, **9.9% pass
undetected**. So on real typing the recall loss would be *smaller* than the typo
rate, and the argument below survives with a different mechanism underneath it.

And the dropped items are the worst possible thing to drop:

[A mistyped national ID is still a national ID sitting in your logs.]{.hl} It is
still personal data, it still identifies a person to anyone who can read it in
context, and it is the case where a user is most likely to send a correction
containing the right number too. A validator configured as a filter deletes
precisely the records a compliance reviewer would care most about.

For calibration on how much work the checksum is doing: a random eleven-digit
string passes it **9,960 times in 1,000,000**, or about **1 in 100**. The
first digit was sampled from 1–9, matching the rule that a TCKN cannot start
with zero, which is why the measured rate lands on 1% — exactly the
$9 \times 10^8$ valid numbers over the $9 \times 10^{10}$ strings with a
non-zero leading digit. Allow leading zeros and the same count over $10^{11}$
strings gives 0.9% instead. That is
strong but not decisive — on a corpus with a lot of numeric strings, the
checksum alone still leaves roughly one false positive per hundred candidates.

### Context recovers what validation loses

The third detector ignores the checksum and asks a different question: is there a
label immediately before the number — `TC kimlik no`, `TCKN`, `kimlik numarası`
— within thirty characters?

Precision **100%**, recall **50.0%**. The recall figure is not a discovery: half
the TCKN-bearing templates in this corpus label the identifier and half leave it
bare, so 50% is the design parameter coming back out. What matters is that the
two detectors fail on *different* items. The checksum misses mistyped
identifiers; context misses unlabelled ones; neither miss implies the other.

So take the union. **Precision 99.1%, recall 93.6%** — nearly all of the
checksum's precision with **three-fifths** of its recall loss recovered: 8.9 of
the 15.3 points, or 32 of the 55 mistyped identifiers.

### Do not validate where the pattern is already unambiguous

The IBAN results say the opposite thing, and the contrast is the actionable part.

```text
IBAN, 120 planted

  detector             hits   correct   precision   recall
  pattern only          120       120      100.0%   100.0%
  pattern + checksum    105       105      100.0%    87.5%
```

`TR` followed by 24 digits does not collide with anything else in this traffic,
so the pattern is already perfect. Adding the ISO 7064 mod-97 check buys **zero**
precision and discards **12.5%** of real IBANs — 15 of 120, this corpus's
realised typo rate for IBANs, and again exactly the mistyped ones.

[Validate where the pattern is ambiguous; do not validate where it is not.]{.hl}
This is the sort of thing that gets applied uniformly because it feels rigorous,
and uniform rigour here is pure loss. The general rule the measurement supports:
**use a checksum to rank confidence, not to filter.** A validated hit is
high-confidence and can be redacted automatically; an unvalidated pattern hit is
lower-confidence and should be redacted too, flagged differently, and reviewed —
not silently dropped.

### What this measurement does not show

Three limits, stated so the numbers are not over-read. The corpus is synthetic
and its decoy density is a choice, so 40% is illustrative rather than
transferable. The typo model is a single random digit, which is kinder than real
mistyping — people transpose, truncate and add spaces. And names, addresses and
free-text disclosures are not covered at all: those need the NER of
@sec-sequence-labeling, they do not have check digits, and they are where a real
Turkish detector will spend most of its difficulty.

## Redaction that you can undo {#sec-guardrails-redaction}

Detection is half the job. What you do with a hit determines whether the product
still works.

Destructive masking — replacing `12345678901` with `[REDACTED]` — is safe and
frequently useless: the agent can no longer look up the order, and the human who
takes over cannot either. **Reversible tokenization** replaces the value with a
stable handle, `[TCKN_1]`, and keeps the mapping in a separate store that the
model never sees. The agent reasons over tokens, tools resolve tokens to values
inside the trusted boundary, and the response is de-tokenized on the way out.

Four properties make this work, and each is a place implementations go wrong:

**Stability within a conversation.** The same value must get the same token, or
the model cannot tell whether two mentions are the same person. Different
conversations should get different tokens, or the token itself becomes an
identifier.

**Format preservation where downstream code cares.** A tool expecting eleven
digits will reject `[TCKN_1]`. Either the tool resolves tokens, or the token
preserves the shape — and preserving shape means the token can be mistaken for
real data, which has to be handled deliberately.

**The mapping is the sensitive asset now.** You have not removed personal data;
you have concentrated it into one store with a join key. That store needs the
retention, access control and residency treatment @sec-governance describes,
and it is a strictly worse breach than the original if it leaks with the
transcripts.

**Redaction happens at one boundary.** @sec-observability made this argument for
telemetry, and it generalises: redact once, before the data reaches anything
that persists it — the model, the trace exporter, the log line, the eval set.
Redacting in five places means five implementations and one of them is wrong.

## Topical guardrails and the cost of being wrong {#sec-guardrails-policy}

Beyond personal data, most products need to keep the system inside a topic:
answer questions about our product, decline medical advice, never speculate
about a competitor's legal problems.

The mechanisms are familiar and layered — a system prompt (cheapest, weakest), a
classifier on input, a classifier on output, and a rule that hard-blocks the
handful of cases you can specify exactly. The layering is worth having; the part
that needs stating is the arithmetic.

[A guardrail's false-positive rate is multiplied by all of your traffic, and its
false-negative rate only by the rare bad case.]{.hl} At 1% false positives and a
million requests a month, ten thousand legitimate users are refused so that a
handful of bad outputs are stopped. Whether that is the right trade depends
entirely on severity, and it should be an explicit decision with both numbers in
front of you rather than a threshold someone picked.

Two consequences follow. **Refuse differently depending on confidence** — a
high-confidence policy hit blocks, a marginal one routes to a human or asks a
clarifying question, and treating those the same wastes the classifier's
information. And **measure the guardrail as a classifier**, with the same
discipline @sec-llm-eval applies to judges: a labelled set of hard cases,
reported precision and recall, and re-measurement after every prompt or model
change, since @sec-production-eval showed how little it takes to move behaviour.

## Classify every action by whether it can be undone {#sec-guardrails-reversibility}

Guardrails on text are the easy half. Once an agent has tools (@sec-tool-design),
the question stops being what it says and becomes what it does — and the
organising principle is reversibility.

| class | examples | default | what to require |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **No state change** | read a record, run a query, draft a message, create a document nobody sees yet | allow | logging only — with the caveat that changing no state is not the same as being reversible: reading data this user is not entitled to cannot be undone once it is in the transcript, so authorisation is a separate axis from this one |
| **Reversible with effort** | update a record, cancel an order, move a file | allow | an audit trail and a documented undo path |
| **Irreversible, bounded** | send an email, post a message, issue a small refund | confirm | approval above a threshold; rate limits |
| **Irreversible, unbounded** | payment, deletion, any external publication, anything touching another person | deny by default | explicit per-action approval, and a limit enforced outside the model |

: A taxonomy that turns "be careful" into configuration
{tbl-colwidths="[18,34,14,34]"}

Three things make this more than a table. **The classification belongs to the
tool, not to the prompt** — it lives in the tool definition, so it cannot be
argued away by a persuasive input. **Bounded and unbounded is the important
line**, and it is enforced by a limit outside the model: an agent that can issue
refunds under €50 is a different risk from one that can issue refunds, and the
difference is a number checked in code. And **defaults are the whole design**:
new tools should land in the strictest class and be relaxed deliberately, because
the alternative is a system whose risk profile is decided by whoever added the
most recent tool.

## Approval gates: interrupt, review, resume {#sec-guardrails-approval}

An approval gate is easy to describe and awkward to build, because it requires
the agent loop to survive being paused for an hour.

The mechanics that matter:

1. **Serialise the pending action, not the conversation.** What awaits approval
   is a specific call with specific arguments — `refund(order=14822,
   amount=780.50)` — and that is what a human must see. Showing them the
   transcript and asking "does this look right?" is not an approval.
2. **Persist enough state to resume.** The loop's state must outlive the process
   (@sec-deployment), or approvals that arrive after a deploy are lost.
3. **Time out explicitly, and decide which way.** An approval that nobody answers
   must expire into a defined outcome. Silent expiry into "denied" strands users;
   into "approved" it is not a gate.
4. **Show the reviewer the evidence, not the conclusion.** The trace (@sec-observability)
   — what the agent read, which tools returned what — is
   what makes a decision possible. A summary written by the same model that
   proposed the action is not independent evidence.
5. **Record the decision as data.** Who approved, when, what they saw. That is
   both the audit trail @sec-governance needs and the labelled set that tells you
   which approvals were rubber-stamped.

That last point is the one that decays. [An approval queue where 99% of items
are approved *may* be oversight working perfectly or a rubber stamp, and the
approval rate alone cannot tell you which.]{.hl} A well-targeted gate in front of
a well-behaved agent should approve almost everything. The measurement that
distinguishes the two is not the rate: seed the queue with items you know are
wrong and count how many reviewers catch. If they catch them, a 99% approval
rate is good news; if they do not, you have a delay with a signature on it.
Track the rejection rate too — a collapse is worth investigating — but audit
with planted errors before you conclude anything from it.

## Kill switches, and undoing what already happened {#sec-guardrails-killswitch}

Everything above is preventive. This section is for when prevention did not work,
and it has two halves that get conflated.

**Stopping.** A kill switch must be operable by someone who did not write the
system, at 3am, without a deploy. That means a runtime flag rather than a code
change, and it needs granularity: stop one tool, one agent, one tenant, or
everything. A single global switch is one people hesitate to pull, and
hesitation at 3am is the failure. Test it on a schedule — an untested kill switch
is a belief.

**Undoing.** Stopping does not reverse the forty actions already taken, and
@sec-deployment's compensating transactions are the mechanism: for every
irreversible tool, a documented inverse or an explicit statement that there is
none. Writing that list is uncomfortable in the useful way, because the entries
that read "no inverse exists" are exactly the tools that need the strictest gate.

Then the ordinary operational hygiene that agents make more urgent: a budget
ceiling per run and per tenant that halts rather than warns; a step ceiling (@sec-deployment)
so a loop terminates; and rate limits per tool, because "the
agent sent 4,000 emails" is a loop, not a decision.

## On-call for agents {#sec-guardrails-oncall}

Agents fail in ways ordinary services do not, and the alert set has to reflect
that. The classic signals — error rate, latency, saturation — stay, and none of
them fire when an agent is confidently doing the wrong thing.

What is worth waking someone for, drawn from what @sec-observability makes
visible:

- **spend rate** above a ceiling, per tenant and per run — the fastest-moving
  failure and the easiest to detect;
- **step-ceiling hits** rising, which means loops;
- **tool error rate** on a single tool, which usually means a dependency changed
  under you;
- **approval queue depth**, because a stalled queue is a stalled product;
- **guardrail trigger rate** moving in either direction — a spike is an attack or
  a bad deploy, a collapse means the guardrail broke;
- **refusal rate**, which is the same signal from the user's side.

A runbook has to answer four questions in the order an on-call engineer needs
them: how do I stop it, how do I tell how bad it is, how do I undo what it did,
and who do I tell. The last one is not administrative — for personal data
incidents there are notification deadlines (@sec-governance), and the clock
starts before anyone has finished diagnosing.

## Postmortems that produce tests {#sec-guardrails-postmortem}

The failure mode of agent postmortems is a specific and boring one: every
finding comes out as "improve the prompt", the document is filed, and the same
class of failure returns in a month.

The fix is to require that each finding produce an artefact that outlives the
document, and there are only a few kinds worth having:

- a **case in the eval suite** that fails before the fix and passes after
  (@sec-production-eval, @sec-agent-eval);
- a **tool reclassified** into a stricter reversibility class;
- a **limit enforced in code** rather than requested in a prompt;
- a **guardrail with a measured threshold**, not a new instruction;
- an **alert** for the signal that would have caught it earlier.

"Improve the prompt" is not on the list. It is unfalsifiable, unversioned in
practice, and @sec-production-eval measured what happens to prompts that are
edited without a gate: a reordering nobody would question moved accuracy by
nearly six times the noise floor.

The blameless part matters more here than in ordinary software, and for a
non-obvious reason. When a system's behaviour is stochastic, the honest finding
is often "the system did something unlikely and our design assumed it would
not" — and that is a *design* finding. A culture that looks for the person who
approved the prompt will get findings shaped like that, and will keep shipping
the design.

## Intuition checks {#sec-guardrails-intuition}

Answer each before you open it. The first is the framing the whole chapter rests
on; the next three carry the measurement; the last two are about oversight
decaying quietly while all the dashboards stay green.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your guardrail catches 99% of policy violations. Is the policy enforced?

No. Against an adversary, 99% is a retry budget.

A guardrail is a probabilistic filter, and someone deliberately trying to get
through gets unlimited attempts against a component that is right most of the
time. That is fine for reducing accidental harm — users pasting things they
should not, models drifting off-topic — and useless as a boundary
(@sec-agent-security).

The architectural consequence: a guardrail belongs in front of a permission
system, never instead of one. If the only thing stopping a large refund is a
classifier that usually notices, the limit is not enforced. Enforce it in code,
outside the model.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your PII regex has 100% recall on the test set. Ship it?

Recall is the number that looks finished; precision is the one that decides
whether anyone can use it.

An eleven-digit regex found all 360 planted Turkish national IDs here — and
**60% of its hits were not national IDs**. Turkish mobile numbers written
without spaces are exactly eleven digits, and so are order references, tracking
codes and meter readings. Separate the two failures, because they cost different
things: a phone number matched by a *national-ID* detector is the wrong type and
usually still personal data you would want redacted, while an order reference is
usually not what you meant to catch, and masking it breaks the support workflow —
though one that can be linked to an identifiable customer can itself be personal
data, so the synthetic fixture's labels do not settle that for real traffic. Driving redaction from
that detector masks the order number the support agent needs; driving alerts from it produces an alert people
ignore within a week.

The 40% precision figure depends on decoy density, which is a property of your
traffic. Measure it on yours before shipping.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Adding the checksum raised precision to 99%. What did it cost?

**15.3 points of recall — and precisely the records you least want to lose.**

The checksum found 305 of 360 planted identifiers, and 305 is exactly the number
that were not mistyped. The recall loss is not approximately the typo rate; it is
the typo rate, mechanically. A mistyped national ID is still a national ID in
your logs: still personal data, still identifying, and often accompanied by a
correction containing the right number.

So use validation to **rank confidence, not to filter**. Validated hits redact
automatically; unvalidated pattern hits still redact, flagged as lower
confidence, and get reviewed rather than dropped. Adding a context check — a
label like `TCKN` shortly before the number — recovers most of the loss, because
it fails on different items: union precision 99.1%, recall 93.6%.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Should you apply the same validation to every identifier type?

No — and IBAN is the counterexample that makes the rule concrete.

`TR` plus 24 digits collides with nothing else in this traffic, so the pattern
alone was **100% precise at 100% recall**. Adding the ISO 7064 mod-97 check
bought **zero** precision and discarded **12.5%** of real IBANs, all of them
mistyped ones.

Validate where the pattern is ambiguous; do not validate where it is not.
Uniform rigour feels principled and is pure loss here. For calibration on how
much the TCKN checksum is doing: a random eleven-digit string passes it about **1
time in 100**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your approval queue approves 99% of what reaches it. Working as intended?

The rate alone cannot tell you. A well-targeted gate in front of a well-behaved
agent should approve almost everything, so 99% may be oversight working — or a
delay wearing oversight's clothes.

Seed the queue with items you know are wrong and count how many reviewers catch.
If they miss them, there are two usual causes. Either the gate is on the wrong
actions (approving things that never needed review, which trains reviewers to
click through) or the reviewers lack what they need to reject anything. The
second is common and fixable: they are being shown a summary written by the same
model that proposed the action, rather than the trace of what it actually read
and called (@sec-observability).

Track the rejection rate as a first-class metric, but read it against the planted
errors. If those get through, fix the gate's scope, show evidence rather than
conclusions, and put the specific pending call in front of reviewers —
`refund(order=14822, amount=780.50)`, not the transcript.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Every postmortem finding says "improve the prompt". What is wrong?

Nothing outlives the document, so the same failure class returns.

Require each finding to produce an artefact: an eval case that fails before the
fix and passes after, a tool moved to a stricter reversibility class, a limit
enforced in code rather than requested in a prompt, a guardrail with a measured
threshold, or an alert for the signal that would have caught it sooner.

"Improve the prompt" is unfalsifiable, and @sec-production-eval measured why it
is also unsafe: reordering a prompt's rules with nothing added or removed moved
accuracy by nearly six times the noise floor. Prompt edits need a gate, not a
resolution in a document.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-guardrails-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the layer

**Q: What is the difference between a guardrail and a security control?**

The adversary. A guardrail reduces harm from a system behaving normally —
unusual inputs, drift, edge cases — and it is a probabilistic filter, so someone
deliberately trying to get past it has unlimited retries against something that
is right most of the time. A security control holds against that. The practical
statement: guardrails go in front of permission systems, never instead of them,
and any limit that matters is enforced in code outside the model.

**Q: How would you detect national ID numbers in Turkish support messages?**

Start with the collision: a Turkish mobile written without spaces is eleven
digits and so is a TCKN, so pattern-only precision was 40% here at 100% recall.
Add the published checksum and precision goes to 99% — but recall falls 15
points, and what it drops is mistyped identifiers, which are still personal
data. So use the checksum to rank rather than filter, and add a context check
for a nearby label, which fails on different items: the union reached 99.1%
precision at 93.6% recall. Then note what none of it covers — names and
addresses have no check digits and need NER.

**Q: How do you decide which agent actions need human approval?**

By reversibility, classified in the tool definition rather than in the prompt so
it cannot be argued away by input. Reversible actions log; reversible-with-effort
actions need a documented undo path; irreversible-but-bounded actions confirm
above a threshold; irreversible-and-unbounded actions deny by default. The line
that does the work is bounded versus unbounded, and it is a number checked in
code — an agent that can refund under €50 is a different system from one that
can refund.

### Testing whether you have operated one

**Q: Your redaction broke the product — agents cannot look up orders any more.
Fix it.**

Two problems, and they need separating. Precision: measure how much of what you
are masking is not the identifier you meant to catch — for an eleven-digit
regex, 60% of hits were not national IDs. Some of those, like phone numbers, are
still personal data, so decide what to mask by data type and context. And
destructiveness: replace masking with reversible tokenization, so the model sees
`[TCKN_1]` while tools resolve tokens to values inside the trusted boundary. Then
say the thing people miss — the token mapping is now the sensitive asset, with
the retention and access controls to match, and a worse breach than the original
if it leaks alongside the transcripts.

**Q: It is 3am and an agent is looping and burning budget. What happens?**

A runbook answers four questions in order: how to stop it, how bad it is, how to
undo it, and who to tell. Stopping is a runtime flag, not a deploy, and it needs
granularity — one tool, one tenant, everything — because a single global switch
is one people hesitate to pull. Undoing is the compensating-transaction list
written in advance, including the entries that say no inverse exists. Telling
matters because personal-data incidents have notification deadlines that start
before diagnosis finishes.

**Q: How do you know your guardrails still work after a model upgrade?**

Treat each one as a classifier with a labelled set of hard cases and re-measure
precision and recall on every model or prompt change, exactly as you would audit
a judge. Then watch two production signals: guardrail trigger rate and refusal
rate, in both directions — a spike is an attack or a bad deploy, and a collapse
means the guardrail silently stopped firing, which no error rate will show you.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-guardrails-tools}

The measurement used no libraries at all — the point was that the hard parts are
the checksum arithmetic and the corpus design, both of which fit in the standard
library. The second table splits into detection and redaction (the first three)
and policy enforcement (the rest).

## Lab: build a guardrail, then measure what it costs {#sec-guardrails-lab}

### Step 1 — build a corpus with planted ground truth

Two hundred messages in your domain, with identifiers planted by construction so
you never hand-label. Include the decoys that actually occur in your traffic —
for Turkish support that means phone numbers, order references and tracking
codes — and mistype a stated fraction of the real identifiers.

### Step 2 — measure the naive detector

Pattern only. Report precision *and* recall, not recall alone. Then read ten of
the false positives and write down what a support agent would lose if each were
masked.

### Step 3 — add validation, and measure what it deletes

Apply the checksum. Report the precision gain and the recall loss, and confirm
whether the recall loss equals your typo rate — if it does, you now know exactly
which records the filter removes, and that they are all real personal data.

### Step 4 — add a second, independent signal

A context check, or an NER model (@sec-sequence-labeling). Measure it alone, then
as a union with the checksum. Be clear about what a union can and cannot do: it
cannot *lower* recall, since it fires whenever either does, but its precision
can move either way, because it inherits both detectors' false positives *and*
both sets of true positives. If A finds one true and one false hit (50%) and B
finds two true hits, one shared with A, the union has two true and one false:
66.7%, above A. So the thing to check is whether the recall it adds is worth
whatever it does to precision —
and if it adds no recall at all, the two signals are failing on the same items
and you need a different second signal.

### Step 5 — make redaction reversible

Replace masking with stable per-conversation tokens and a mapping the model never
sees. Verify the agent can still complete a lookup task end to end. Then write
down where the mapping lives, who can read it, and how long it is kept.

### Step 6 — classify your tools and enforce one limit in code

Put every tool in the four-class taxonomy. Take the riskiest one, add a numeric
limit enforced outside the model, and confirm by test that a prompt asking
nicely cannot exceed it.

### Step 7 — pull your own kill switch

In staging, stop one tool at runtime with no deploy, and time it. Then list the
irreversible actions that were in flight and how each would be undone. Entries
with no inverse are your findings.

### What to hand in

Precision and recall for all four detector configurations on your own corpus;
ten false positives with what each would have cost; evidence that reversible
redaction preserves task completion; your tool classification with one limit
enforced in code and a test proving it; and the timed kill-switch result with
your compensating-action list.

## Exercises {#sec-guardrails-exercises}

1. **Precision on real traffic.** Run an eleven-digit detector over a week of
   your own logs and hand-check fifty hits. Report precision, and compare it to
   the 40% measured here on synthetic decoy density.

2. **The typo question.** Mistype 15% of the identifiers in your test corpus,
   each by replacing exactly one digit with a different digit, then confirm that
   your validator's recall loss equals that rate. (The equality holds only for
   single-digit substitutions; adjacent transpositions can pass the check.) Decide, and
   write down, what your system should do with an unvalidated pattern hit.

3. **Where validation is pointless.** Find an identifier type in your domain
   whose pattern is already unambiguous. Measure whether its checksum buys any
   precision. If it does not, remove it and report the recall you get back.

4. **Reversible redaction, end to end.** Implement tokenization and have an agent
   complete a task that requires resolving a token through a tool. Then write the
   threat model for the mapping store in one paragraph.

5. **The reversibility audit.** Classify every tool in a system you run. Report
   how many are irreversible and unbounded, and how many of those have a limit
   enforced outside the model.

6. **Approval rejection rate.** Instrument your approval gate and measure what
   fraction is rejected. Then seed the queue with items you know are wrong and
   count how many reviewers catch. A high approval rate is a defect only if
   planted errors get through; if they do, diagnose which of the two causes it
   is and fix that one.

7. **Guardrail regression.** Take a guardrail classifier, build a labelled set of
   forty hard cases, and re-measure it after changing the model behind it. Report
   the change in precision and recall.

8. **The 3am runbook.** Write the runbook for "the agent is looping and burning
   budget", then have a colleague who did not write the system execute it against
   staging while you time them. Every question they have to ask you is a gap.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-guardrails-deeper}

Before reading: take your PII detector, if you have one, and measure its
precision rather than its recall. Which number your team can quote is a good
indicator of which one it optimised.

This chapter cites no papers, so there is one table rather than the usual two.
The adversarial side of this material — where guardrails stop being sufficient —
is @sec-agent-security, and its sources are there.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [`presidio`](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio) | the production version of this chapter's measurement: recognisers, context enhancement, checksum validators and reversible anonymisation, all readable |
| [`llm-guard`](https://github.com/protectai/llm-guard) | a bundle of input and output scanners; useful mostly for reading what a reasonable default set contains |
| [`NeMo-Guardrails`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Guardrails) | policy as dialogue flows rather than prompt text, which is a genuinely different design point |
| [`guardrails`](https://github.com/guardrails-ai/guardrails) | validators over structured output with re-asking, the enforcement counterpart to @sec-decoding |
| [`PyRIT`](https://github.com/Azure/PyRIT) | red-teaming automation; the fastest way to find out what your guardrails miss, and the bridge to @sec-agent-security |

## What to remember {#sec-guardrails-summary}

- **A guardrail is not a security boundary.** It reduces harm from a system
  behaving normally; it fails probabilistically and quietly, and an adversary
  gets unlimited retries against it. [Guardrails go in front of permission
  systems, never instead of them]{.hl} — any limit that matters is enforced in
  code, outside the model.

- **Report precision *and* recall, and price both errors.** An eleven-digit
  regex found 100% of planted Turkish national IDs and **60% of its hits were
  not national IDs**, because a Turkish mobile written without spaces is also
  eleven digits. A missed identifier is a leak; an unnecessary redaction is a
  support agent who cannot see the order number. Recall is the number that looks
  finished, and precision is usually the one that decides whether the people who
  have to use the guardrail keep it switched on.

- **Validation buys precision and deletes real personal data.** The TCKN checksum
  took precision from **40.0% to 99.0%** and recall from 100% to **84.7%** — and
  the 15.3-point loss is mechanically equal to the corpus's typo rate. [A
  mistyped national ID is still a national ID in your logs.]{.hl}

- **Use a checksum to rank confidence, not to filter.** Validated hits redact
  automatically; unvalidated pattern hits still redact, flagged lower-confidence,
  and get reviewed rather than dropped. A random eleven-digit string passes the
  TCKN check about **1 time in 100**.

- **Combine signals that fail differently.** The checksum misses mistyped
  identifiers; a context word misses unlabelled ones. Their union reached
  **99.1% precision at 93.6% recall** — nearly all of the checksum's precision
  with three-fifths of its recall loss recovered: 8.9 of the 15.3 points.

- **Do not validate where the pattern is unambiguous.** `TR` + 24 digits was
  already **100% precise**, so the IBAN checksum bought nothing and discarded
  **12.5%** of real IBANs. Uniform rigour is pure loss here.

- **Redact reversibly, and know what you have created.** Stable per-conversation
  tokens keep the product working where destructive masking breaks it — but the
  token mapping is now the sensitive asset, and it is a worse breach than the
  original if it leaks with the transcripts. Redact once, at one boundary.

- **Classify actions by reversibility, in the tool rather than the prompt.** The
  line that does the work is bounded versus unbounded, enforced by a number
  checked in code. New tools land in the strictest class and are relaxed
  deliberately.

- **Oversight decays quietly.** [An approval queue that approves 99% of what
  reaches it may be oversight or a delay, and only planted errors tell you
  which]{.hl} — seed known-wrong items and count how many reviewers catch, track
  the rejection rate, show reviewers the pending call and the trace rather than a
  model-written summary,
  and watch guardrail trigger rate in both directions, since a collapse means it
  broke and no error rate will tell you.

- **Every postmortem finding must outlive the document.** An eval case, a tool
  reclassified, a limit in code, a measured threshold, an alert. "Improve the
  prompt" is not on the list — @sec-production-eval measured a prompt reordering
  moving accuracy by nearly six times the noise floor.
